p.src: As they journeyed onward, they suddenly saw a walled city close ahead. Tripitaka reined in his horse and called, “Disciples, look! What place is that?” Pilgrim said, “Master, so you cannot read after all! How ever did you accept the Tang emperor’s command and leave his court?” Tripitaka said, “I have been a monk from childhood and am versed in countless sutras and scriptures. How can you say I cannot read?” Pilgrim said, “If you can read, why ask what place it is when three great characters are plainly written on the apricot-yellow banner above the city wall?” Tripitaka scolded him: “You impudent monkey, what nonsense! The banner is whipping wildly in the wind. Even if there are characters on it, they cannot be read clearly.” Pilgrim said, “Then how is it that old Monkey can see them?” Bajie and Friar Sand said, “Master, do not listen to our elder brother’s tricks. At such a distance we cannot even make out the city clearly. How could he already see what characters are written there?” Pilgrim said, “Do they not read ‘Kingdom of Scarlet and Purple’?” Tripitaka said, “The Kingdom of Scarlet and Purple must be a sovereign realm of the Western Regions. We shall have to exchange our travel rescript there.” Pilgrim said, “Enough talk, then.”

p.src: As master and disciples made their way along the great market street, they saw dignified people in neat attire whose speech was clear and refined. The place truly yielded nothing to the realm of Great Tang. The merchants on both sides suddenly noticed Zhu Bajie’s ugly features, Friar Sand’s dark face and towering frame, and Sun the Pilgrim’s hairy face and jutting brow. Abandoning their business, they all crowded round to stare. Tripitaka kept warning them, “Do not cause trouble. Keep your heads down and walk.” Bajie obeyed, tucking his lotus-pod snout against his chest; Friar Sand dared not look up; only Pilgrim looked this way and that while keeping close beside the Tang Monk. Those with good sense watched for a while and then went home. But the idlers and unruly children came surging forward amid laughter, tossing tiles and bricks to make sport of Bajie. Tripitaka broke into a cold sweat and kept saying, “Do not start anything.” The fool dared not raise his head.

p.src: Before long they rounded a street corner and suddenly saw a walled gateway bearing the three characters “Bureau of Foreign Reception.” The Tang Monk said, “Disciples, let us enter this government office.” Pilgrim asked, “What for?” The Tang Monk replied, “The Bureau of Foreign Reception is where travelers from all under heaven meet and are received, so we too may impose upon its hospitality. Let us rest inside while I attend the king, have our travel rescript exchanged, and then hurry out of the city to continue our journey.” At this Bajie thrust out his snout, frightening several dozen of the onlookers so badly that they fell over. He stepped forward and said, “Master is right. Let us hide ourselves inside and escape the racket of these wretched creatures.” They accordingly entered the bureau. Only then did the crowd gradually disperse.

p.src: Now, the bureau had two commissioners, a chief and a deputy. Both were in the main hall checking the attendants who were to go out and receive an official. Suddenly seeing the Tang Monk arrive, they were both startled and cried together, “Who are you? Who are you? Where are you going?” Tripitaka pressed his palms together and said, “This poor monk was commissioned by His Majesty of Great Tang in the Eastern Land to journey to the Western Heaven and fetch the scriptures. Having now reached your honored realm, I dare not pass through without leave. I have a travel rescript that must be inspected and exchanged before I may proceed, and ask only to rest temporarily in your noble office.” Hearing this, the two commissioners dismissed their attendants, straightened their caps and belts, and came down from the hall to greet him properly. They immediately ordered a guest room cleaned for their repose and instructed that plain vegetarian provisions be supplied. Tripitaka thanked them. The two officials led their attendants out of the hall and departed. Their subordinates invited the venerable master to rest in the guest room, and Tripitaka went with them. Pilgrim complained bitterly, “What lazy wretches! Why would they not let old Monkey stay in the main hall?” Tripitaka said, “This land is neither subject to our Great Tang nor joined to our country. Moreover, superior officials and traveling guests are constantly passing through, so it would not be proper for them to entertain us here.” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, I shall make them entertain us.”

p.src: While they were speaking, a steward brought their provisions: a tray of white rice, a tray of white flour, two handfuls of green vegetables, four pieces of bean curd, two pieces of wheat gluten, a tray of dried bamboo shoots, and a tray of wood-ear mushrooms. Tripitaka told his disciples to accept them and thanked the steward. The steward said, “There is a clean stove and cooking pot in the west room, with firewood ready to hand. Please prepare your own meal there.” Tripitaka asked, “May I ask you one thing: is the king in the audience hall?” The steward replied, “His Majesty has long ceased to hold court. Today, however, is an auspicious day, and he is now consulting his civil and military officials about issuing a proclamation. If you wish to have your travel rescript exchanged, hurry there now and you may still catch him; tomorrow it will be impossible, for no one knows how long it may be before he next appears.” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, you all prepare the vegetarian meal here. I shall hurry to have our rescript inspected, then return so that we may eat and be on our way.” Bajie quickly took out the cassock and the travel rescript. Tripitaka made himself presentable and set out for court, repeatedly warning his disciples not to go outside and cause trouble.

p.src: Before long he reached the Tower of Five Phoenixes. No words could exhaust the soaring grandeur of its halls and the magnificence of its towers and terraces. He went straight to the outer End Gate and asked the reporting officer to convey to the Celestial Court his wish to have his travel rescript inspected and exchanged. The palace herald duly went before the jade steps and reported: “Outside the court gate is an imperial envoy of Great Tang in the Eastern Land, a monk bound for the Thunderclap Monastery in the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. He wishes to exchange his passport and awaits Your Majesty’s summons.” The king was delighted to hear this and said, “I have long been ill and have not ascended the throne to hold court. Today, just as I take my seat in the hall to issue a proclamation seeking a physician, a holy monk arrives in my kingdom.” He at once issued an edict summoning him to the foot of the steps. Tripitaka immediately bowed and prostrated himself. The king then summoned him into the Golden Hall, bestowed a seat upon him, and ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainment to prepare a vegetarian feast. Tripitaka thanked him for the favor and presented the travel rescript.

And as for the Tang emperor, what illness caused him to return from death, and why did he send you across distant mountains and rivers to seek the scriptures?” Questioned thus, the elder monk rose slightly from his seat, pressed his palms together, and said, “In this poor monk’s homeland:

p.src: Hearing this, the king suddenly gave a groan and asked, “Master, from what country did that worthy minister come?” Tripitaka replied, “He was none other than the chief minister at my sovereign’s court, whose surname was Wei. He understood astronomy, knew geography, and discerned the workings of yin and yang; truly, he was a great minister capable of securing a realm and establishing a nation. Because he beheaded the Dragon King of the Jing River in a dream, that dragon king brought suit in the underworld, saying that my sovereign had promised to save him but then caused his death. My sovereign therefore fell gravely ill and gradually felt his life drawing into peril. Wei Zheng then wrote a letter for my sovereign to carry into the underworld, addressed to Judge Cui Jue in the city of Fengdu. Before long, the Tang emperor died, but after three days he returned to life. It was thanks to Wei Zheng, who persuaded Judge Cui to alter the records and add twenty years to the emperor’s life. Now he wishes to hold a Great Rite of Water and Land, and so he sent this poor monk on a long journey through many realms to worship the Buddha and obtain the three collections of Mahayana scriptures, that souls suffering for their sins might be delivered and ascend to Heaven.” The king groaned again and sighed, “Yours is indeed a great celestial empire, with an upright ruler and worthy ministers. But I have been ill for so long, and not one of my ministers has been able to save me.” Hearing this, the elder stole a glance and saw that the emperor’s face was sallow, his body wasted, his form gaunt, and his vitality spent. Just as the elder was about to ask him more, an officer of the Court of Imperial Entertainments submitted a request that the Tang monk be served his vegetarian meal. The king issued an order: “Set it out in the Hall of Fragrant Draperies together with my own meal, so that I may dine with the Master.” Tripitaka thanked him for his favor and ate his vegetarian meal with the king; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Sun the Pilgrim, back at the Court of Interpreters, told Sha Monk to prepare tea and rice and make ready some vegetarian dishes. Sha Monk said, “Tea and rice are easily cooked, but the vegetables are harder to prepare.” “Why is that?” asked the Pilgrim. Sha Monk replied, “We have no oil, salt, soy sauce, or vinegar.” The Pilgrim said, “I have a few coins here from alms. Let Bajie go out to the market and buy them.” The idiot, seeking to shirk the errand, said, “I dare not go. My face is none too handsome, and I fear I may cause trouble and be blamed by Master.” The Pilgrim said, “You will be trading fairly, neither begging from them nor robbing them. What trouble could there be?” Bajie said, “Didn’t you see what happened just now? When I stuck my snout out before this gate, I frightened a dozen or so people to the ground. If I went into the crowded market, who knows how many people I might frighten to death?” The Pilgrim said, “You noticed only the crowd in the market. Did you see what wares were being sold there?” Bajie replied, “Master told me to keep my head down and not get into trouble, so I truly saw nothing.” The Pilgrim said, “Never mind the wine shops, rice stores, mills, silk merchants, and general stores; there were also fine teahouses and noodle shops, great baked flatbreads and big steamed buns. The eating houses had excellent rice in broth, fine peppery seasonings, and good vegetables, as well as unusual sugar cakes, steamed pastries, snacks, stuffed dumplings, fried foods, and honeyed sweets—countless delicacies. How would you like me to buy some for you?” At this the idiot’s mouth watered, and he gulped his saliva noisily. Leaping to his feet, he said, “Brother, I’ll let you treat me this time. When I have saved some money, I’ll return the feast.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly and said, “Sha Monk, cook the rice well and wait while we go and buy the seasonings.” Sha Monk too knew that he was teasing the idiot, so he merely played along: “Off you go, then. Be sure to buy plenty, and come back with full stomachs.” The idiot grabbed a bowl and followed the Pilgrim out through the gate. Two officials on duty asked, “Where are you going, venerable sirs?” “To buy seasonings,” replied the Pilgrim. One of them said, “Go west along this street and turn the corner by the Drum Tower. At the Zheng family’s general store you may buy as much as you please; they have oil, salt, soy sauce, vinegar, ginger, pepper, and tea leaves, all in stock.”

p.src: The two went off hand in hand, supporting each other as they headed straight west along the street. The Pilgrim passed several teahouses and a number of eating houses, yet bought nothing where there was food to buy and ate nothing where there was food to eat. Bajie called out, “Elder Brother, let’s just buy something here and make do with it.” But the Pilgrim had intended all along to tease him and would not buy anything. “Dear brother, you really do not know how to shop. Let us walk a little farther and choose a large place to buy our food.” As the two talked on, they drew another great crowd, who followed them and jostled for a look. Presently they reached the Drum Tower, where they saw a countless throng clamoring below it, packed shoulder to shoulder and blocking both street and road. At the sight Bajie said, “Brother, I’m not going any farther. They are making a great uproar over there. I fear they may be arresting monks; and since we are suspicious strangers, what would we do if they seized us?” “Nonsense!” said the Pilgrim. Monks have broken no law. Why should they arrest us? Let us go through and buy some seasonings at the Zheng family’s shop.” Bajie said, “No, no, no! I am not getting myself into trouble. If I squeeze into that crowd and my ears swipe a couple of people, frightening them into stumbling and scrambling until several are trampled to death, I’ll have to pay with my life!” The Pilgrim said, “Very well. Stand here by the foot of this wall and wait while I go over and make the purchases. I’ll buy you some vegetarian noodles and flatbread to eat.” The idiot handed the bowl to the Pilgrim, pressed his snout against the foot of the wall, turned his face away, and would not move for anything.

p.src: Well done, Great Sage! He bent down, dropped the bowl, picked up a pinch of earth and tossed it into the air. Muttering an incantation, he made himself invisible, stepped softly forward, and took down the proclamation. Facing southeast, he drew in a breath of immortal air and blew it forth, raising a whirlwind that scattered everyone. Then he turned back and went straight to where Bajie stood. There he saw the idiot with his snout pressed against the foot of the wall, seemingly fast asleep. Without disturbing him, the Pilgrim folded the proclamation and gently tucked it into his robe. Then he turned on his heel and went back ahead of him to the Court of Interpreters; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now when the people below the tower saw the wind rise, they each covered their heads and shut their eyes. When the wind had passed, they found the imperial proclamation gone, and all were terrified. The proclamation had been brought out after the morning court by twelve eunuchs and twelve palace guards. It had hung there for less than six hours when the wind swept it away, and as they searched all around in trembling alarm, they suddenly saw the edge of a sheet of paper protruding from Zhu Bajie's robe. They came forward and asked, “Was it you who took down the proclamation?” The fool jerked up his head and thrust out his snout. The sight so frightened the guards that they staggered backward and fell to the ground. He turned to leave, but several bolder men blocked his way and seized him, saying, “You have taken down the imperial proclamation calling for a physician. Instead of entering the palace to cure His Majesty, where do you think you are going?” The fool said in a fluster, “Your son took down the proclamation, and your grandson knows how to cure him!” A guard asked, “Then what are you carrying inside your robe?” Only then did the fool look down, and sure enough there was a written sheet there. He unfolded it, looked, and cursed through clenched teeth, “That monkey has done me in!” With an angry growl, he made to tear it apart. u.src: Now when the people below the tower saw the wind rise, they each covered their heads and shut their eyes.

The fool jerked up his head and thrust out his snout.

p.src: Before long the commotion stirred the whole neighborhood, and a crowd gathered around him. Among them were two elderly eunuchs, who said, “Your appearance is strange and your voice sounds peculiar. Where have you come from, to behave with such boorish obstinacy?” Bajie replied, “We were sent from the Great Tang in the East to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Our master is a monk and sworn younger brother of the Tang emperor. He has just entered the palace to have our travel documents endorsed. My elder brother and I came here to buy seasonings. Seeing so many people below the tower, I did not dare approach, so my brother told me to wait here. But when he saw the proclamation, he raised a whirlwind and tore it down, secretly stuffed it into my robe, and left ahead of me.” One eunuch said, “Earlier I saw a plump, fair-faced monk heading straight for the palace gate. Would that be your master?” Bajie said, “That is he, that is he.” The eunuch asked, “Where has your elder brother gone?” Bajie replied, “There are four of us in our party. While Master has gone to have our travel documents endorsed, the three of us, together with our luggage and horse, are lodging at the Huitong Hostel. After playing this trick on me, my elder brother returned to the hostel first.” The eunuch said, “Guards, stop pulling him. We shall all go to the hostel, and there we will learn the truth.” Bajie said, “You two grannies have some sense.” The guards said, “This monk truly knows nothing! Why does he keep calling the eunuchs ‘grannies’ instead of ‘honored sirs’?” Bajie laughed. “Shameless creatures! You have reversed yin and yang. These two are old mothers. Instead of calling them grannies or grandmothers, you call them grandfathers?” The others said, “Enough of your cheek. Hurry and take us to your elder brother.”

p.src: The noisy crowd in the street numbered not merely three or five hundred, and together they bore him all the way to the hostel gate. Bajie said, “Everyone, stop here. My elder brother is not like me; he will not let you make sport of him. He is a fierce and earnest fellow. When you see him, you must bow deeply and address him as Lord Sun. Then he will receive you; otherwise he will change his countenance, and the whole affair will come to nothing.” The eunuchs and guards all said, “If your elder brother truly has the skill to cure the king, he deserves half the realm, and it is only proper that we bow to him.”

p.src: The idle onlookers all remained outside the gate, clamoring noisily. Bajie led the party of eunuchs and guards straight into the hostel. He heard the Pilgrim and Sha Monk in their guest room, laughing and joking about how the proclamation had been taken down. Bajie rushed forward, grabbed the Pilgrim, and shouted wildly, “Can you call yourself a decent man? You tricked me into going to buy vegetarian noodles, flatbread, and steamed buns for myself, but it was all an empty promise. Then you raised a whirlwind, tore down some imperial proclamation, secretly stuffed it into my robe, and used me as your dupe. Is that how a brother should behave?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “You fool, you must have taken the wrong road and wandered somewhere else. I passed the Drum Tower, bought the seasonings, and hurried back to look for you. When I could not find you, I returned here first. Where would I have taken down any imperial proclamation?” Bajie said, “The officials charged with watching the proclamation are standing right here.” Before he had finished, the eunuchs and guards came forward, bowed to the Pilgrim, and said, “Lord Sun, our king is blessed today, for Heaven has sent Your Lordship down to us. We beg you to display your masterly skill and apply your well-tested medical art. If you cure our king, half the realm shall be yours, and the state itself shall be divided with you.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim assumed a grave expression, took the proclamation from Bajie, and asked the men, “I suppose you are the officials charged with guarding the proclamation?” The eunuchs kowtowed and said, “Your servants are palace eunuchs of the Directorate of Ceremonial. These men are guards of the Embroidered Uniform Guard.” The Pilgrim said, “It was indeed I who took down this proclamation seeking a physician, and I deliberately sent my junior brother to introduce me. Since your ruler is ill, as the saying goes, ‘Good medicine is not lightly sold, and the sick must seek the physician.’ Go and tell the king to come here in person to invite me. I possess the power to cure his illness the moment I lay hands on it.” The eunuchs were all appalled when they heard this. The guards said, “One who dares speak so boldly must surely possess great ability. Let half of us remain here to await him in silence, while the other half enter the palace and report to the throne.”

p.src: They immediately assigned four eunuchs and six guards, who, without waiting to be summoned, went straight into court and reported from the foot of the steps, “Ten thousand joys to Your Majesty!” The king had just finished dining and was conversing with Tripitaka. On suddenly hearing this report, he asked, “Whence comes this good news?” The eunuchs reported, “This morning your servants took out the royal proclamation seeking a physician and posted it beneath the Drum Tower. It was taken down by Elder Sun, a holy monk who has come from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch the scriptures. He is now at the Court of Receptions and asks that Your Majesty invite him in person, for he possesses the power to cure a disease as soon as he lays hands upon it. That is why we have come especially to report this.” The king was delighted to hear this and immediately asked the Tang Monk, “How many worthy disciples have you, Master?” Tripitaka put his palms together and replied, “This poor monk has three unruly disciples.” The king asked, “Which of your worthy disciples is skilled in medicine?” Tripitaka said, “To tell Your Majesty the truth, those unruly disciples of mine are all merely rustic bunglers. They know only how to carry the baggage, lead the horse, cross ravines in search of water, and guide this poor monk over mountains and ridges. When we reach some perilous place, they may subdue demons and capture monsters, seize tigers and tame dragons, but not one of them knows anything of the properties of medicines.” The king said, “Why be so modest, Master? That I should hold court today and fortunately meet you here is truly a bond ordained by Heaven. If your disciple knows no medicine, why would he take down my proclamation and demand that I welcome him in person? He must surely possess the ability to heal a sovereign.” He called out, “My civil and military ministers, I am weak in body and feeble in strength and dare not ride in my palanquin. Go outside the court in my stead and respectfully invite Elder Sun to come and examine my illness. When you meet him, you must on no account slight him. Address him as ‘Holy Monk Elder Sun,’ and receive him with all the ceremony due between sovereign and minister.”

p.src: The ministers accepted the decree and went straight to the Court of Receptions with the eunuchs and guards who had watched the proclamation, where they formed ranks and bowed in homage. This frightened Eight Rules into hiding in a side room, while Sha Monk slipped behind a wall. But the Great Sage watched them from his seat in the middle, sitting upright and perfectly still. Eight Rules secretly grumbled, “That macaque will be the death of us with his outrageous behavior! How can he let so many officials bow to him without returning their salutes or even rising to his feet?” Before long the homage was complete, and the officials separated into ranks and announced, “We address Holy Monk Elder Sun: we are all ministers of the King of the Scarlet-Purple Kingdom. By royal command, we respectfully offer you due ceremony and invite the holy monk to enter the court and examine His Majesty’s illness.” Only then did the Pilgrim rise and ask them, “Why has your king not come?” The ministers replied, “Our king is weak in body and feeble in strength and dares not ride in his palanquin. He has therefore specially ordered us to perform the sovereign’s ceremony in his stead and bow before the holy monk to invite you.” The Pilgrim said, “If that is so, gentlemen, please lead the way. I shall follow you there.” The ministers proceeded in companies according to their ranks. The Pilgrim straightened his robes and rose. Eight Rules said, “Brother, whatever you do, don’t drag us into this.” The Pilgrim replied, “I won’t drag you in. I only want the two of you to receive medicines for me.” Sha Monk asked, “What medicines are we to receive?” The Pilgrim said, “Whatever medicines anyone brings for me, accept them in the stated quantities and keep them until I return to use them.” The two agreed, and we shall speak no more of them.

Let us report once more.” The attendant went into the palace again and reported, “My lord, Elder Sun says that without seeing Your Majesty’s face, he can diagnose your pulse by suspended threads.” The king thought to himself, “I have been ill for three years, yet have never tried such a method. Summon him in.” The attendant hurriedly conveyed the order: “His Majesty has consented to let him diagnose the pulse by suspended threads. Quickly summon Elder Sun into the palace to make his examination.”

p.src: The Pilgrim then ascended the jeweled hall. The Tang Monk met him and scolded, “You wretched monkey, you have ruined me!” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Dear Master, I am bringing you honor, yet you claim I am harming you?” Tripitaka shouted, “In all these years you have followed me, whom have I ever seen you cure? You know nothing of the properties of medicines and have never read a medical book. How could you be so bold as to bring this great calamity upon us?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Master, it seems you did not know. I have several rustic prescriptions that can cure grave illnesses. I guarantee I shall make him well. Even if I doctor him to death, I could only be charged as a quack who killed a man, and that is not a capital crime. What are you afraid of? It is nothing serious, nothing serious. Just sit down and see how well I understand the pulse.” The elder continued, “Have you ever seen what passages are contained in the Basic Questions, the Classic of Difficult Issues, the Materia Medica, and the Pulse Formula, or how they are explained? You talk such wild nonsense—what could you know of diagnosing the pulse by suspended threads?” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “I carry golden threads on my person. You have simply never seen them.” He immediately reached down, plucked three hairs from his tail, twisted them in his hand, and cried, “Change!” They at once changed into three silken cords, each twenty-four feet long in correspondence with the twenty-four seasonal divisions. Holding them in his hand, he said to the Tang Monk, “Are these not my golden threads?” A nearby attendant eunuch said, “Elder, enough boasting. Please enter the inner palace and make your examination.” The Pilgrim took leave of the Tang Monk and followed the attendant into the inner palace to examine the illness. And so it was that:
